**Setup.** Write M = r/(s−1). A remainder T ∈ [0, M] can take digit a exactly when T ∈ J_a = [a/s, (a+M)/s]. Every T in [0, M] has at least one expansion. So T has a unique expansion exactly when every successive remainder lies in a "forced" region, where only one digit is available.

**Forced intervals.** Removing the overlaps J_a ∩ J_{a±1} from J_a gives:
- F_0 = [0, 1/s)
- F_a = ((a−1+M)/s, (a+1)/s) for 1 ≤ a ≤ r−1
- F_r = ((r−1+M)/s, M]

**Transitions.** The map T ↦ sT − a sends F_a to (M−1, 1) for 1 ≤ a ≤ r−1. Let q = r−s+1. Then M−1 = q/(s−1) > q/s, so F_{q−1} lies outside this image, while F_q, …, F_{s−1} lie fully inside it. The image of F_0 is [0, 1), which contains F_0, …, F_{s−1}. The image of F_r is (M−1, M], which contains F_q, …, F_r. Every F_b contained in an image is covered completely, so the transitions are full.

**Recurrent core.** The set C = {F_q, …, F_{s−1}} is closed under transitions, and every state in C reaches every state in C. It has s−q = 2s−1−r states. F_0 and F_r are transient and feed into C. The unique-expansion set is therefore a graph-directed self-similar set whose essential part has an all-ones transition matrix of size 2s−1−r.

**Dimension.** The number of surviving cylinders at level n grows like (2s−1−r)^n, and each has length of order s^(−n). Hence

dim_H(U_{s,r}) = log(2s−1−r) / log s.

- For s = 3, r = 3, the core is F_1 and F_2, giving log 2 / log 3.
